title: Finding Federal Recompetes Early: A 12-24 Month Guide
summary: Find federal recompetes 12 to 24 months before the RFP: five signals, a lead screen, and a capture-to-proposal handoff.
body_markdown:
If your recompete pipeline starts at RFP release, you're not really competing for most of those deals. The incumbents who consistently win knew the opportunity was coming years earlier. This guide shows where to find recompetes 12 to 24 months before the solicitation, how to qualify them, and how to carry what you learn into the proposal.


**TLDR:**


- Incumbents usually start a recompete with the edge, and much of it comes from positioning done long before the solicitation.
- Start sourcing 12 to 24 months out: use USAspending.gov and contract award data in SAM.gov (formerly FPDS) to find contracts whose current end date matches their potential end date, a sign no options remain.
- Five signals point to a likely recompete: options used up, extensions past the last option, sources sought or RFI notices, agency forecast entries, and signs of incumbent trouble.
- Qualify leads against NAICS alignment, incumbent vulnerability, set-aside status, agency relationship depth, and past performance before committing capture hours.
- Capture work only pays off if it reaches the proposal team: keep win themes on the opportunity and build the annotated outline from them.


## Why Recompetes Belong at the Top of Your BD Pipeline


By the time an RFP posts on SAM.gov, the challenger is filing paperwork for a deal the incumbent has already shaped.


A pursuit that begins at solicitation release gives you weeks to build what the incumbent spent years developing: agency relationships, past performance aligned to the requirement, and a technical approach that mirrors how the work is actually done. Closing that gap means finding opportunities 12 to 24 months out, before requirements are drafted and evaluation criteria are set. That is the first step in a disciplined[federal capture planning process](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/federal-capture-planning-process) .


Recompetes carry less unknown risk than new work: the requirement is documented, the budget exists, and the timeline is predictable, so your capture dollars go further. Many competitors also start late. That front-loaded research also has a staffing cost:[Precise Software](https://www.goveagle.com/case-study/precise-software-case-study) , a federal IT contractor, cut SME time on early-stage proposals by 80% after moving early research off senior leaders' desks. Savings like that free capture hours for a 12 to 24 month lead time.


## How Federal Contracts Are Structured: The Recompete Window


Many federal services contracts follow a base-period-plus-option-years structure, typically a one-year base with multiple one-year options. The end date on any given award reflects only where the agency currently sits in that sequence, not the contract ceiling.


That distinction matters for recompete tracking. A contract showing an end date 14 months out may still have unexercised options. Many contracts require the agency to give preliminary notice of its intent to extend, typically 60 days before expiration, and the decision to exercise an option rests on performance, continued need, and available funding. Once the final option year nears exhaustion, a new competitive procurement is typically required.


Agencies often begin pre-solicitation activity 12 to 18 months before the final period ends. By the time a sources sought or RFI posts, requirements are often already taking shape around the incumbent's solution. Find the contract before that stage and you can still help shape the requirement.


## The Five Signals That a Recompete Is Approaching


Not every expiring contract becomes a competitive recompete. Some roll into bridge extensions; others get sole-sourced. These five signals help show which path an award is on.


### 1. No Remaining Option Years


Pull the award in USAspending.gov and compare the current end date with the potential end date, which assumes every option is exercised. If the two match, no options usually remain, and the contract has nowhere to go except a new procurement or a bridge. Short extensions under FAR 52.217-8 are themselves options, so confirm in the modification history. If the end date is 12 to 24 months out and no options remain, treat it as a recompete candidate.


### 2. Extensions Past the Last Option


Extensions past the last priced option suggest the agency is running behind on the recompete. Many contracts allow extensions of up to six months under FAR 52.217-8. Longer bridges are often new sole-source awards, and the agency posts the justification on SAM.gov. Serial extensions often mean a solicitation is overdue and being planned. Check the modification history in SAM.gov contract award data.


### 3. Sources Sought or RFI Notices


A sources sought posted by the contracting office suggests the agency is testing the market for a new award. Watch[SAM.gov](https://sam.gov/opportunities) for these notices against the NAICS codes and agencies where you track active awards.


### 4. Agency Procurement Forecasts


Many agencies publish procurement forecasts on the Acquisition Gateway or their own procurement pages; check both, since many DoD forecasts sit outside the Gateway. An entry for the same requirement, program office, and dollar range as an expiring contract shows the agency is planning a new award. Check whether it is listed as a competition, a set-aside, or a directed award.


### 5. Signs of Incumbent Trouble


CPARS ratings aren't public (this[CPARS guide](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/cpars-past-performance-proposal-guide) covers how they work), so challengers have to work from other signals. A termination for default shows in contract award data and in SAM.gov's responsibility and qualification records, though defaults are rare. More often, the signal is turnover in the incumbent's key personnel, or concerns the customer raises at industry days and one-on-ones. Any of these can open the door in a best-value competition where the agency wants a change.


## Where to Find Expiring Federal Contracts: Primary Data Sources


Four public sources do most of the work, and paid tools like GovWin IQ build on them. None gives the full picture alone.


### USAspending.gov


[USAspending.gov](https://www.usaspending.gov/) is the starting point for finding contracts by end date. Search by agency, NAICS code, or awarding office, then download or sort the results by end date to pull contracts ending in your target window. Check two dates on each award: the current end date and the potential end date. A gap usually means options remain; confirm in the modification history before you draw conclusions about recompete timing.


### SAM.gov Contract Awards (Formerly FPDS)


FPDS.gov search was retired on February 24, 2026, and contract award data now lives in SAM.gov, which requires a free login. Use it to check what USAspending surfaces: pull the modification history and look for option exercises, extensions, and ceiling increases. Repeated extensions with no options left point to an overdue recompete.


### SAM.gov


Use[SAM.gov](https://sam.gov/opportunities) notices to confirm leads you already have. By the time a sources sought or presolicitation notice posts, the agency is already in active acquisition planning. A sources sought tied to a contract you are already monitoring is a strong signal the recompete is moving.


### Acquisition Gateway Forecast Tool


The[Acquisition Gateway Forecast Tool](https://acquisitiongateway.gov/forecast) surfaces planned procurements agencies have self-reported, including follow-on requirements. Cross-reference entries against known expiring awards to see whether an agency is planning a new competitive action or extending the incumbent.


## Reading a Recompete Lead: A Signal-to-Source Mapping Table


The table pairs each signal with where to find it and what it means for capture. Use it to sort likely recompete leads from contracts that still have runway.


Signal Where to Find It What It Tells Capture


Current end date 12 to 24 months out USAspending.gov (sort or download by end date) Contract is entering the recompete window; check the potential end date before treating it as a live lead


No options remaining USAspending.gov (current vs. potential end date) and SAM.gov modification history Incumbent has no runway left; a new procurement is likely


Extension past the last option SAM.gov contract award data (modification history) Agency is behind on the recompete; a solicitation is likely overdue and in planning


Sources Sought or presolicitation notice SAM.gov opportunity search by NAICS and agency Agency is conducting market research; a new award is likely in planning


Agency forecast entry matching an expiring award Acquisition Gateway Forecast Tool Agency has self-reported a follow-on procurement; cross-reference against known incumbents


Termination for default or key personnel turnover SAM.gov contract award data and responsibility records; LinkedIn Incumbent may be vulnerable; worth a closer look before committing capture hours


## Using the Federal Recompete Outlook to Build a Lead List


As of November 2026, at least 1,072 federal prime contracts with $100M or more obligated reach the end of their current period of performance by April 2028, carrying about $465B in obligations to date. The Department of Defense accounts for 660 of those awards. GovEagle built the[Federal Recompete Outlook](https://www.goveagle.com/federal-markets/recompetes) as a starting point for this kind of sourcing work.


Every entry is a research lead for a possible recompete, follow-on, or extension, not a confirmed competitive procurement. Dollar figures reflect obligations to date, not contract ceilings. With about half ending within six months, the list needs triage before it is useful.


For firms that aren't already incumbents on large operating contracts, the best targets usually sit in mid-market services: IT modernization, professional services, and mission support contracts in the $100M to $500M range. Large operating contracts tied to national labs or major sustainment programs are typically held by a handful of large primes with incumbency advantages that make challenger positioning difficult. Use the report's agency and NAICS pages to isolate work that fits your footprint.


The report's linked contractor profiles are where sourcing gets specific. Pull the expiring award, identify the current prime, and cross-reference against your own NAICS positioning. If the incumbent holds multiple expiring awards in your target codes, you have both a competitive picture and a teaming signal worth pursuing before any solicitation posts.


Run the same checks on your own expiring awards. If you hold contracts on the list, the signals in this guide are the ones your competitors are watching.

## Qualifying and Ranking Recompete Leads


An expiring-contract list without a qualification pass is a distraction, not a pipeline. Without a qualification layer tied to a disciplined[opportunity pipeline strategy](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/govcon-opportunity-pipeline-strategy) , it becomes a watchlist that consumes BD hours without producing decisions.


Run each lead against these five checks:


- NAICS and scope alignment: does the requirement match how you actually perform work, beyond simply how you're registered?
- Incumbent vulnerability: key personnel turnover, repeated extensions, or customer concerns you hear firsthand all shift[PWin](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/what-is-pwin-probability-of-win-guide) in your favor.
- Set-aside status: recompetes can change socioeconomic designations. A contract that ran full-and-open (open to all bidders) may recompete as a small business set-aside, or the reverse. Check the likely future status before committing capture resources.
- Agency relationship depth: do you have an existing program office contact, or are you starting cold?
- Past performance relevance: can you cite work of comparable scope, complexity, and dollar value in the same mission area?


Run those five checks, the same kind of screen built into[bid/no-bid analysis tools](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/bid-no-bid-analysis-tools-government-contractors) , before assigning capture hours. A contract that clears all five is a live pursuit. One that fails on scope or past performance relevance goes in a passive monitor file.


Every team has a limit on how many recompetes it can pursue well at once, set by team size, pursuit complexity, and capture resources. Spreading across twenty expiring contracts with no qualification criteria produces shallow research on all of them. Rank leads early, before a solicitation exists.


## Incumbent Research: What Public Data Reveals


Public data on the incumbent is more useful than most challengers treat it. Accessed early enough, it shapes how you position your solution before a single requirement is written.


Start with USAspending.gov. The award record shows obligations to date against the potential award amount, which tells you how the agency actually used the contract. For example, a hypothetical contract with a $200M potential value but $80M obligated suggests scope compression or budget constraints worth understanding before you price a follow-on.


USAspending's sub-award records show the first-tier subcontractors the prime has reported, which gives you a view of the teaming structure. Obligation and modification trends across option years show how the work grew or shrank. Neither source shows labor rates, so obligation trends are one input to your price-to-win range, not the incumbent's actual prices.


CPARS ratings are not public, and a debrief only covers your own proposal. Look for terminations and key personnel turnover instead, and listen to what the customer says about the current work.


Track the incumbent's program manager and technical lead on LinkedIn and at industry days. Turnover in either role after year two of a five-year contract is a relationship gap the incumbent may struggle to close before the next evaluation panel.


All of this feeds your ghosting strategy: proposal language that points out a competitor's weaknesses without naming them. Performance gaps tell you which strengths to prove. Teaming structure reveals capability gaps you can fill with a stronger sub. The earlier this research starts, the more it shapes agency engagement, solution framing, and the questions you ask before requirements are drafted.


## The 12-to-24-Month Capture Timeline for a Recompete Pursuit


The timeline has three phases. The research from each phase has to reach the proposal team.


### 18 to 24 Months Out: Identification and Research


This is sourcing work. Pull the expiring award, identify the incumbent, map the program office contacts, and log what public data reveals about scope, pricing history, and performance. Assign a preliminary PWin score based on your NAICS alignment, past performance depth, and relationship standing, work that falls squarely within[what a capture manager does](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/what-does-capture-manager-do) at this stage. Most of this phase is passive intelligence gathering. But decisions made here, like whether to pursue solo or seek a teaming partner, carry through every later phase.


### 12 to 18 Months Out: Agency Engagement and Positioning


Active capture begins here. Schedule agency meetings, attend industry days, and submit RFI responses that position your approach. Run incumbent gap analysis against the modification history and what the customer tells you. Finalize teaming decisions and begin price-to-win scoping, the kind of work that can[raise PWin before RFP release](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/raise-pwin-before-rfp-release) . This phase produces the capture artifacts proposal teams need most: win themes, competitive assessment, and a defensible pricing range.


### 6 to 12 Months Out: Solution Shaping and Draft Anticipation


Sources sought notices or draft RFPs may begin surfacing. Use them to pressure-test your technical approach against requirements as they take shape and run internal color team preparation against the expected Section L (instructions) and Section M (evaluation criteria), where the solicitation uses them. Capture work shifts to proposal readiness in this phase.


The persistent risk across all three phases is the handoff. Win themes developed at month 18, competitive intelligence gathered at month 12, and solution decisions made at month 8 all have to reach the proposal team in a usable form. Often it lives in a capture manager's notes, a CRM record nobody reads, or a debrief slide that never gets attached to the opportunity, the exact fragmentation that[unifying GovCon opportunity tracking](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/govcon-opportunity-tracking-capture-intelligence) is meant to solve.


## Carrying Recompete Intelligence Into the Proposal


Win themes get lost in the shuffle between capture and proposal. Capture intelligence gathered over 18 months compresses into a debrief slide, a CRM note, or a conversation the proposal manager never attended. By the time writers open a blank technical volume, the win themes are gone.


What needs to transfer is specific: the incumbent's pricing history and performance vulnerabilities, your teaming rationale and how each partner fills a documented gap, agency relationship context including which program office contacts shaped the requirement, and the price-to-win (PTW) range and its assumptions. Writers need the artifacts themselves attached to the opportunity when drafting begins.


An annotated outline mapped to Section L and M requirements is the practical mechanism for carrying that context forward. When each outline section references the capture-stage win theme it needs to express, writers start with strategic direction already embedded, and the outline serves as the handoff document.

## Final Thoughts on Building a Recompete-Driven BD Pipeline


The research tools are all public, and the signals are consistent once you know what to look for. Start in USAspending and SAM.gov contract data 18 months out, qualify leads against NAICS alignment and past performance depth, and build agency relationships before requirements are drafted. ## FAQ


### How do you find federal recompetes 12 to 24 months before a solicitation posts?


Start with USAspending.gov filtered by NAICS code and agency and sorted by end date, then compare each award's current and potential end dates and check the modification history in SAM.gov contract award data. Layer in SAM.gov sources sought notices and the Acquisition Gateway Forecast Tool to see which expiring awards look headed for a new competition, not a bridge or sole-source award. The goal is to get to the opportunity before requirements are drafted and evaluation criteria are locked around the incumbent's solution.


### What signals confirm an expiring federal contract is a genuine recompete candidate and not a bridge or extension?


Look for several signals together: no options left (the current and potential end dates match in USAspending), extensions past the last option in the modification history, a sources sought or presolicitation notice on SAM.gov from the same program office, and a matching entry in the Acquisition Gateway Forecast Tool. Signs of incumbent trouble, such as a termination for default or key personnel turnover, add to the case. One signal is a reason to monitor; several together are a reason to assign capture hours.


### How do I carry capture intelligence from an 18-month recompete pursuit into the proposal without losing it at handoff?


Win themes, competitive assessments, and pricing assumptions gathered during capture typically compress into a CRM note or debrief slide that proposal writers never see. The practical fix is an annotated outline mapped to Section L and Section M requirements where each section references the specific win theme and capture-stage competitive context it needs to express, so writers start with strategic direction already embedded instead of reconstructing it from scratch. GovEagle supports this by storing win themes on each opportunity and building an annotated outline mapped to Section L, M, and PWS requirements.


### How can I tell whether an expiring federal contract still has options left?


Open the award in USAspending.gov and compare the current end date with the potential end date. The potential end date assumes every option is exercised, so if the two dates match, no options usually remain and a recompete, bridge, or extension is coming. If they differ, the contract still has runway. Confirm with the modification history in SAM.gov contract award data, which shows each option exercise and extension.


### Can I use public data to assess incumbent vulnerability before a recompete solicitation posts?


Yes. USAspending.gov shows obligations against the potential award amount, which can reveal scope compression or budget constraints worth accounting for in pricing. Its sub-award records show the first-tier subcontractors the prime has reported. CPARS ratings are not public, so look instead for terminations for default in SAM.gov records and for turnover in the incumbent's program manager or technical lead, since a departure after year two of a five-year contract is a relationship gap the incumbent may struggle to close before the next evaluation panel.
